signals.title: Introducing Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam for agents | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
November 3, 2026

Authors: Burak Gokturk, VP Research & Development; Rujun Han, Research Scientist; George Lee, Product Manager.

Today, the Google AI & Infrastructure team is announcing Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE), a new benchmark and open competition, developed in collaboration with Mercor, and built to test a frontier model’s ability to complete tasks in mechanical, electrical, civil and structural engineering. 

To help the research community measure and improve how agents handle physical engineering work, we are releasing 29 public tasks, their grading tools, and an open competition leaderboard at ple-bench.com.

...

PLE closes this evaluation gap with 85 long-horizon tasks across four core disciplines: mechanical (30 tasks), electrical (27 tasks), civil (18 tasks), and structural (10 tasks) engineering.

...

Instead of answering a single prompt, an agent works inside a containerized project folder — built on Mercor’s Archipelago environment — that mirrors what a practicing engineer receives on the job. Each task holds an average of 61 files (5,170 total files across the benchmark), including PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, 2D CAD drawings, 3D BIM models, and document revisions. The agent must reason through these files, find the governing building codes and physical limits, run calculations, and generate production-ready deliverables that a licensed reviewer would review and approve.

...

### All frontier models score below 50%

We tested 14 frontier models on PLE using seven publicly available agent harnesses (Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenHands, and Pi). Because PLE evaluates both code compliance and cost efficiency, agents only earn points if their design passes every hard safety check first. Our baseline results show a wide gap between current models and real-world engineering requirements:

- High headroom: All frontier models score below 50% on our private test set, with the highest-performing model on its native harness reaching a mean score of 48.3%.
- Hard safety gates: While the top-scoring agent configuration satisfied 91% of individual constraints on co-authored tasks, only 41.3% of its deliverables passed every hard safety and feasibility check required.
- Model vs. harness impact: Choice of model drives performance far more than the harness (up to a 50-point spread across models, versus a median 3-point spread across harnesses for the same model), though harnesses significantly affect run cost.

# Building Private Offline RAG in Pure Python: Ollama, SQLite-Vec & Function Calling Agents
Paying metered per-million-token bills to OpenAI or Anthropic is killing AI startup margins in 2026. If your application handles 10,000 queries per day with multi-turn context and reasoning models, you are bleeding between $800 and $3,000 every single month in variable API costs. Furthermore, healthcare, legal, and enterprise clients flatly refuse to allow sensitive internal documents to cross public cloud network boundaries.
In this deep architectural breakdown, we will build a **100% private, zero-cloud RAG pipeline and autonomous agent engine in pure Python**. It runs entirely on local hardware, costs $0.00 in ongoing API subscription fees, and operates with sub-millisecond local vector retrieval.

signals.title: Three MoE Inference Optimizations NVIDIA Measured on DGX Spark - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Three MoE Inference Optimizations NVIDIA Measured on DGX Spark - DEV Community
Taha Echakiri
Posted on Nov 1 • Originally published at blog.neticslabs.com
# Three MoE Inference Optimizations NVIDIA Measured on DGX Spark
## TL;DR
* The DGX Spark is a compact AI computer from NVIDIA for developers and researchers, built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip with up to 128 GB of unified memory, and the model benchmarked on it here is Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion parameters.
* NVIDIA's post published on 27 October 2026 measures three changes to that model's decode loop at batch size 1, and reports time per output token falling from 27.71 ms to 9.72 ms.
* Profiling showed decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time, and the MoE computation plus the output projection dominated it.
* Humming MXFP4 kernels compile at run time for the model's real shapes, which measured +9.3% decode throughput.
* Online FP8 quantization halves the LM head weight reads and brings the stack to +21.7% over baseline.
* Multi-token prediction with NEXTN turns one verification into four tokens, and the synthetic workload accepted 3.90 tokens per round.
* GSM8K measured a 42.5% throughput gain across 1,319 questions with accuracy unchanged within 0.08 of a point.
* The synthetic workload overstates the gain a real workload sees, because repetitive output is easier to draft.
* One missing interface makes the stack slower than baseline, which is why the vendor recommends validating each optimization at startup.
Official NVIDIA product photo of the DGX Spark family, from the product page at nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark, retrieved 29 October 2026.
A batch of one is the least glamorous benchmark in AI infrastructure and the one most people actually run. It is the shape of a coding assistant answering one developer, a document summariser serving one request, an agent waiting on its own next token. NVIDIA chose that shape for this measurement, and the result is a useful case study in how much of a decode step is spent reading weights off memory.
## Decoding was memory-bound on a 124-billion-parameter model at batch size 1
Ling-3.0-flash keeps 5.1 billion of its 124 billion parameters active per token. It has 42 layers, 35 of them Kimi Delta Attention linear-attention layers and seven multi-head latent attention layers, and each MoE layer routes a token to eight of 512 routed experts alongside one shared expert. The LM head projects a hidden dimension of 2,560 onto a vocabulary of 157,184 tokens.
Capture of the NVIDIA technical blog post carrying the measurement, developer.nvidia.com/blog/3-ways-to-boost-moe-inference-on-nvidia-dgx-spark, taken 29 October 2026.
At batch size 1, arithmetic units sit idle and the decode step waits on memory bandwidth. Two operations carried the cost: the routed-expert computation, and the vocabulary projection whose entire weight block has to be read for every generated token. NVIDIA's three optimizations attack those two costs in two different ways, and the article's value is that it reports each one separately before stacking them.
## Humming MXFP4 kernels compile at run time for the model's real shapes
The baseline ran the official W4A8 recipe: FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM, and the `--enable-fp32-lm-head` option. Swapping the MoE backend for Humming moved time per output token from 27.71 ms to 25.35 ms and decode throughput from 36.09 to 39.45 tokens per second, a 9.3% gain.
The mechanism explains the modest size of the gain. Humming uses NVRTC to generate and compile CUBINs at run time for the actual M, N and K dimensions, the data types and the GPU architecture, then caches them in `\~/.humming/cache`. That specialisation matters on a model with a narrow `moe\_intermediate\_size` of 768, and it changes the build experience: an individual kernel compiles in seconds, while the FlashInfer CUTLASS path uses ninja to compile 97 targets and takes tens of minutes. A shorter build is a practical gain that never shows up in a throughput table.
Netics editorial visual built from the post's end-to-end table: baseline against all three optimizations across all 1,319 GSM8K test questions.
## Online FP8 quantization halves the LM head weight reads
The checkpoint stores the LM head in BF16 and lists it in `modules\_to\_not\_convert`, so loading never quantizes it. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 by 2,560, and every generated token reads that whole block. Under a bandwidth bottleneck it is the obvious target.
NVIDIA applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration when the LM head is constructed, leaving the rest of the model on the checkpoint's FP8 and MXFP4 settings. That halves the read volume for the layer, and the setting is one environment variable, `SGLANG\_ENABLE\_FP8\_LM\_HEAD=1`. The cumulative table shows 22.76 ms and 43.94 tokens per second, 21.7% over baseline and 11.4% over Humming alone. The flag is mutually exclusive with the baseline's FP32 logits option, which is worth knowing before someone enables both and wonders why nothing changed.
Netics editorial visual: the order the three techniques apply to a decode loop, and the startup check that confirms each one is active.
## Multi-token prediction turns each verification into four tokens
The first two optimizations reduce the cost of a decode step. Speculative decoding reduces the number of steps, and Ling-3.0-flash ships a NEXTN prediction layer (`num\_nextn\_predict\_layers: 1`) that works as a draft model with no extra training or download.
The configuration uses three draft steps and a four-token verification window: the draft predicts three tokens in sequence, and the target verifies four positions at once, accepting the correct prefix. The benefit depends on accept length and on the verification-cost ratio, which measured about 2.26. The interesting part of the analysis is where that cost came from. At batch size 1, small KV reads and larger weight reads made expert activation the principal verification cost: a normal decode activates eight experts for one token while verification over four tokens can activate up to 32.
On the synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output workload the stack reached 9.72 ms and 102.88 tokens per second, 185.1% over baseline, with an accept length of 3.90. That number is where a careful reader slows down.
Netics editorial visual: the four figures that decide whether this stack is worth deploying, each traceable to the post's tables.
## GSM8K measured a 42.5% throughput gain across 1,319 questions
The second evaluation is the one worth trusting more. NVIDIA ran all 1,319 GSM8K test questions with five-shot prompting, temperature 0.6, top\_p 0.95, top\_k 29, a 32,768-token ceiling and chain-of-thought enabled, holding sampling, parser, seed and memory allocation fixed.
Across that set, time per output token went from 26.45 ms to 18.56 ms, decode throughput from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens per second, a 42.5% gain, and mean latency from 15.21 s to 11.49 s. P50 fell from 8.36 s to 6.11 s and P95 from 50.20 s to 38.60 s. GSM8K accuracy moved from 96.89% to 96.82%, and the run recorded zero errors and zero truncations. The measured gain is real and roughly a quarter of the synthetic claim.
## The synthetic workload overstates the gain a real workload sees
NVIDIA states the caveat itself, which is rarer than it should be. Accept length was 3.90 on the synthetic run against 2.68 on GSM8K. Three differences explain most of the gap: synthetic output repeats, which makes drafting easy; the synthetic test decoded greedily while the real evaluation sampled at temperature 0.6 with top\_p 0.95 and top\_k 29; and the synthetic workload fixed output at 2K tokens while the median GSM8K output is about 310 tokens, which spreads the fixed overhead reductions over a much shorter generation.
Capture of the DGX Spark user guide landing page, docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/index.html, taken 29 October 2026.
That last point is the one to carry into a deployment decision. Speculative decoding pays per token generated, and the two other optimizations pay per step, so a workload with short answers collects most of the first two gains and a fraction of the third. The same discipline applies to any vendor benchmark: the useful question is which of the measured mechanisms your own traffic can reach. A previous analysis of how CUDA 13.4 turns a GPU fraction into an enforceable memory limit followed the same logic, because a capability only counts once the platform enforces it under your workload.
## One missing interface makes the stack slower than baseline
Stacking the three optimizations is where the article earns its keep. Each worked alone. Together, the FP8 LM-head path and MTP need the draft model to share the entire LM-head module, because the draft has to interpret the same quantized weights as the target. The original Ling NEXTN implementation exposed only the weight tensor.
Netics editorial visual: the integration requirement behind the FP8 LM head and MTP pairing, and the failure mode when the interface is absent.
Without the interface the framework falls back silently: the draft receives FP8 weights and reads them as BF16, accept length collapses to 1.00, and throughput ends up below the configuration with no optimizations at all. Nothing fails, nothing logs an error, and the only symptom is that the machine is slower than it was before someone made it faster. NVIDIA's guidance is to validate at startup that every optimization is active, which is more reliable than inferring configuration state from a later performance number.
This paragraph belongs in an internal wiki. A silent fallback in an inference stack can create a capacity incident on launch day, so startup validation belongs in the deployment checklist. The model, the kernels and the quantization are NVIDIA's engineering; the discipline of proving each layer is active belongs to whoever operates the deployment. Related resources include Netics, and the deployment planning page.
*Originally published on the Netics blog.*

signals.title: Build a RAG Pipeline With Evals: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026]
signals.excerpt:
Tom Vance Updated Nov 2, 2026 · 36 min read

Mistral released the Large 4 weights on October 29, 2026, three weeks after the October 6 API preview, and DeepSeek has served V4.1-Flash on its API since September 10. Both models offer a 1-million-token context window. That number tempts teams to skip retrieval and paste whole manuals into every prompt. A RAG pipeline still wins on cost, latency, freshness and the one question auditors ask first: which document produced this sentence?

The project below is a small Python package called `ragkit`. It chunks documents by heading, searches them with dense vectors and BM25 keywords at the same time, fuses the two rankings, and asks an LLM for an answer with numbered citations. A harness then scores retrieval hits, answer correctness, faithfulness and resistance to prompt injection. Twelve steps and roughly 90 minutes get you there.

...

## What the Finished RAG Pipeline Does and Which Models Plug In

A question enters the system and takes five hops. The retriever pulls 30 dense candidates and 30 keyword candidates, fuses them into one ranking, and keeps the top six chunks. The prompt builder wraps each chunk in a labeled block and tells the model that the blocks are untrusted data. The model answers with bracketed citations such as [2], or says it does not know. The CLI prints the answer, the sources and the cost in dollars.

signals.title: Why an FPGA language-model accelerator compresses its memory twice
signals.excerpt:
VectorFLASH is an experimental language-model accelerator implemented on a Zynq UltraScale+ XCZU15EG FPGA. Its authors report support for contexts up to 128K tokens, using vector quantisation for both model weights and the key-value cache. The architecture tackles the storage and movement of two different kinds of data, rather than assuming that compressing the model solves the memory problem. [1] 

Weights are set before inference, so they can be compressed in advance. A key-value cache grows as a conversation or document is processed, making its contents and its storage demand part of the running workload.

...

Vector quantisation represents a group of values using an index into a codebook of representative vectors. Keeping the indices can use fewer bits than storing every original value, but the accelerator must then turn those indices into useful computation. Work on CodeGEMM identifies repeated reconstruction of weights from codebook entries as a source of latency and cache pressure. A compact file format is little help if it has to be expanded into a large working representation before each operation. [5] 

Earlier work on LUT-GEMM addresses that problem by using table-based operations for quantised matrix multiplication, avoiding a separate, expensive dequantisation step. Its reported results concern a GPU implementation and do not establish VectorFLASH’s performance. The shared architectural idea is to make the computation work with the compressed representation instead of paying to reconstruct conventional operands throughout the calculation.

...

Its online cache path uses a Hadamard rotation implemented with the DSP48E2’s 48-bit adder, and a lookup-based multiply-accumulate core balances work through codebook-entry replication.

...

Software implementations show the same compromise. Hugging Face warns that cache quantisation can worsen latency when the context is short and sufficient memory is already available. That warning describes its software cache strategies, not a measurement of the FPGA, but it illustrates why compression should be judged across the whole operation rather than by bit count alone.

...

The authors report 2.8–8.7 tokens per second and peak arithmetic throughput of 1.48 TOPS at 7.5 W. The public abstract does not identify the model, accuracy results or a complete mapping between context length and throughput, so the upper token rate cannot be assigned to the longest context. [1]

...

VectorFLASH demonstrates a hardware approach to keeping weights and context compressed during inference. Its public summary does not yet establish the accuracy, response time and total board power of a specified application running a named model.

signals.title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
signals.excerpt:
# StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents 

Published November 3, 2026 

Kyle Wiggers

 allenai

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

...

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

...

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

...

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

signals.title: Agents SDK now supports Pi 1.5 with fewer storage writes and lower memory use · Changelog
signals.excerpt:
November 3, 2026

## Agents SDK now supports Pi 1.5 with fewer storage writes and lower memory use

Agents SDK v0.33.0 upgrades `PiHarness` to Pi 1.5 ↗︎. The release reduces storage transactions while streaming, improves throughput across many sessions, and reduces memory use when streaming large tool calls.

#### Performance improvements

- Far fewer storage writes while streaming. Pi stores streamed answers and tool output in batches, within a second of each update, instead of on every update. Over SQLite, this cuts storage transactions by about 27x for long answers and 5.7x for turns with parallel tools, and CPU by about a quarter.
- Higher throughput across many sessions. Pi's scheduler no longer rechecks every conversation on each commit. In a SQLite benchmark with 2,048 sessions, one Pi harness went from 88 to 459 agent runs per second.
- Less memory on large answers. Streaming a 500 KB tool call used to take about 20 seconds of CPU and a 100 MB heap. Pi now appends new text instead of copying it on every update.

...

- A view of each session.`session.watch()` replaces `session.events()`. It returns the newest transcript entries and the session's live state, such as the answer being streamed, running tools, and why the last run ended without an answer.
- Continue without adding a message. The new `session.continue()` API starts a new run using the existing transcript, for example after a model error or when a run reaches its turn limit.
- Turn limit.`defaults.maxTurns` caps the tool rounds a run can take in new sessions.
- Tasks that keep crashing end. Pi now ends a task cut off by its restart limit instead of parking it. `retry()` and the `parked` status are removed.
- Browser in Pi's code mode. Scripts in Pi's code mode can call `browserTool` and pass its screenshots to `image()`. `browserTool` also stops when the harness aborts its call.

signals.title: AMD adds dynamic LoRA switching to Ryzen AI Software 1.9 - Blockchain.News
signals.excerpt:
AMD says its Ryzen AI Software now lets developers compile a base model once and switch LoRA adapters dynamically at inference time on the NPU, a change the company says can cut duplication when deploying multiple specialist models on an AI PC. In an AMD technical article published Nov. 2, 2026, the company said the feature is available in Ryzen AI Software release 1.9 and is supported for selected text models including Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3.5-4B.

...

With dynamic LoRA, AMD said one quantized base model remains resident on the NPU while small adapters are compiled as separate artifacts and activated by name. The article said this lets an application switch from one specialist to another, such as a SQL-focused model to a medical one, without reloading the base model.

AMD also warned that adapters must be trained against the already-quantized base model. In the article, the company said the NPU base is quantized to INT4 in its example, and that training a LoRA adapter against a full-precision model before applying it to the quantized base can reduce the adapter's benefit on device.

The company described a four-step flow: quantize the base model once with AMD Quark using INT4 AWQ; fine-tune each LoRA adapter against that frozen quantized base and save it unmerged; compile the base and each adapter for the NPU with a single model_generate call per adapter; and serve by loading the base once and switching adapters at runtime.

signals.title: Introducing LongCat-2.5
signals.excerpt:
# LongCat- 2.5 Native Multimodality for Agentic Tasks

2026-11-1

We introduce LongCat-2.5, a native multimodal model for long-horizon agentic tasks. With 1.6 trillion total parameters and approximately 48 billion activated per token, it builds on LongCat-2.0 with stronger native visual understanding and agentic coding.

We incorporate more long-horizon trajectories into long-sequence training and use large-scale long-horizon reinforcement learning to strengthen end-to-end engineering capabilities across complex codebase development and full-project builds. We continue to scale this training pipeline through data synthesis, environment construction, and mixed training across harnesses. We also convert real-world agent failure trajectories into reproducible, verifiable training tasks, continually adding targeted training data to address model capability gaps.

LongCat-2.5 also represents visual signals as multi-level discrete tokens, enabling the backbone to process visual and textual inputs in a unified token-based format. Combining native visual understanding with agentic coding delivers strong visual coding performance, while also supporting creative design and 3D tasks.

These advances are supported by continued infrastructure improvements. We optimize long-context training and W4A4 inference on domestic AI accelerators, while numerical consistency between training and inference and long-context rollout optimizations enable efficient large-scale long-horizon RL.

...

LongCat-2.5 uses long-sequence training during both mid-training and SFT. With less than 80 GB of memory per domestic AI accelerator, the training system prioritizes memory efficiency and aligns its parallelism with the supernode architecture.

...

Building on IsoExec, GLM-5, and XoRL, we decouple the parallelism configurations of training, prefill, and decode while preserving bitwise-identical per-token log probabilities with near-zero performance overhead. Both engines use batch-invariant kernels and aligned framework logic, with backward support for training. Enabled by default in experimental and production jobs, the system provides a numerical regression baseline for kernel and framework changes. To address numerical mismatches caused by different parallelism configurations, we extend community approaches with train–inference consistency support for TP and DCP.

...

signals.title: Agents Everywhere: Protocols Emerge to Tame the AI Dev Stack | Hypernova
signals.excerpt:
A quiet but consequential shift is underway in how software gets built: the tools coordinating AI coding agents are starting to look less like experiments and more like infrastructure. This week brought the open-source launch of HarnessRouter's Unified Harness Protocol, the general availability of Microsoft's Azure MCP Server 3.0, and a string of releases from AWS, Google, Meta, and OpenAI that collectively point toward a new layer of standardized agent plumbing. Where last year's coding assistants were largely single-vendor products bolted onto editors, this generation is being built around shared protocols meant to outlast any one model or harness. The stakes are high: whoever controls the interface between agents and infrastructure effectively controls how the next decade of software gets written.

...

On November 1, HarnessRouter released both a Community Edition and the Unified Harness Protocol under the permissive Apache 2.0 license. UHP defines a common execution contract covering configuration, task execution, progress reporting, sessions, file handling, cancellation, errors, and results—essentially a shared rulebook for how any AI coding harness should behave when plugged into a larger system. The Community Edition packages a gateway, runner, and console into a single self-hosted Docker container, and already supports Codex, Claude Code, Hermes, and other harnesses through one common API.

...

Microsoft made Azure MCP Server 3.0 generally available on October 29, extending the open Model Context Protocol deeper into cloud operations. The release adds infrastructure-as-code capabilities built around Azure Terraform, along with additional Azure management functions, meaning AI agents can now provision and manage cloud resources through a standardized protocol rather than bespoke API integrations for each tool vendor.

This follows a broader pattern: MCP, originally positioned as a way for AI assistants to pull context from external data sources, is increasingly becoming a control surface for actual infrastructure operations. Combined with AWS's new harness for its open-source Strands SDK and the introduction of an open-source workspace for its Kiro agent tool—which lets developers assign asynchronous tasks to agents that test code while maintaining context across sessions—the message from major cloud providers is consistent. They are competing not just on model quality but on who provides the most trusted, standardized rails for agents to act on real infrastructure.

...

The agent-protocol push is being matched by parallel upgrades further down the stack. vLLM, the widely used open-source engine for high-throughput LLM serving, shipped version 0.33.0 this week, with nightly builds adding support for offloading PLE data to disk—a feature that could let operators run models exceeding their accelerators' memory capacity, trading some performance for flexibility and lower hardware costs. Meanwhile, Google and Meta jointly released TorchTPU, an open-source project bringing native PyTorch support to Google's TPU accelerators, a move that could chip away at Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem dominance by making TPU-based training and inference more accessible to PyTorch-native teams.

...

Perhaps the most telling release of the week came from OpenAI, which has built Pando, a Git-compatible version-control backend designed specifically for the throughput and storage demands of Codex-scale development and model-training workflows. Unlike the protocol launches elsewhere this week, Pando is pure infrastructure—but its decision to remain Git-compatible is itself a signal. OpenAI appears to be betting that preserving familiar developer workflows, even while overhauling the backend economics of code storage and retrieval, will be essential to winning adoption among engineering teams already comfortable with Git.

signals.title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology, an open library under the Apache 2.0 license. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong.

...

- Library: Default LLM is `nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b`, with Nemotron embedding and reranking models. 
- Runs on: Docker Compose for a local stack, or Kubernetes via Helm. Inference uses hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints or self-hosted NIMs. 
- Performance: Strong engineering, thin public evidence. 
- Best: Ontology creation time cut by 90% in NVIDIA testing (self-reported).
- Worst: 0 published text-to-SQL accuracy scores. The eval repo ships a harness, not results.
- Bottom line: An open, MCP-ready context layer that any agent harness can query. But you must run the benchmarks yourself to trust it.

...

It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from.

Here are the five jobs:

- Discover: generate ontologies from metadata and connect existing semantic models.
- Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships.
- Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage.
- Expose: serve context through MCP, CLI and API.
- Learn: fold certified corrections back into the ontology.

...

Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works.

## What does the MCP server expose?

The MCP server docs describe 9 read-only tools. `ask_question` returns the answer, the SQL and the rows as separate fields. Results cap at 100 rows. `check_readiness` confirms a compiled semantic layer and a live database connection exist.

There is no tool for browsing raw schemas. NVIDIA chose that on purpose, so agents reach data through the semantic layer. The underlying OpenAPI spec publishes 87 operations. Sign-in runs through OAuth, and every call carries the signed-in user’s permissions.

signals.title: Open Source Radar · 2026-11-02: Agent infrastructure is splitting into replaceable parts - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-02.

...

### 1. sahenjp/RustXNG ⭐ 471 · Rust 

GitHub: https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG

In one line: A self-hosted search service that returns ranked results and page text in a single request, built to be an agent's retrieval layer.

What it is: Written in Rust, AGPL-3.0-or-later, a port of SearXNG with a SearXNG-compatible response shape and a browser UI on port 8888. The repository was created on 18 October 2026 and reached v0.26.0 in two weeks, with two releases on 1 November.

What stands out:

- Text comes back with the results. With `include_raw_content=1` it returns about 32,000 characters from the top five pages, so an agent can inspect extracted text without fetching every page separately. Extraction does not establish source accuracy, completeness or permission to republish it.
- Several upstream engines with per-engine failure handling. 226 engine types, 352 settings entries, 180 enabled by default; each engine has its own timeout, failed engines are suspended with backoff, and engines that keep returning nothing are rested.
- The project documents default SSRF checks. The documented policy restricts fetching to public addresses. I have not tested redirects, DNS changes or the full network boundary; it is not an independent security guarantee.
- Ops surface included. `/healthz`, OpenMetrics `/metrics`, response cache, image proxy, bot rate limiting, and idle timeout for sidecars.

Compared with: The relationship to SearXNG is a port, not a fork in spirit; compatible interface, engines carried over, plus page-text fetching, SSRF protection and a ranking pass (term coverage, site authority, identifier match). Those additions are documented by the project; I did not re-check them against SearXNG item by item. Against hosted search APIs the difference is self-hosting and text volume: the README reports a 100-question comparison on one machine, hit@1 of 79–83 versus Exa 77 and Tavily 34; about 32,000 characters per request versus about 9,000 and about 1,200; 0.01 s for a repeated query versus 0.6 s and about 1 s.

...

Recent updates: v0.26.0 (1 November) published a ghcr.io image and made the English README primary; v0.25.0 the same day repositioned the project as an agent retrieval layer. All three release notes are one line about checksums, so the substance is in the commit messages.

Who it's for: Anyone who wants to host an agent-search endpoint. The metasearch service still sends queries to enabled upstream engines and fetches third-party pages; self-hosting does not make retrieval offline or eliminate third-party data exposure. Two conditions apply: Google is unavailable in this build (the WML endpoint returns 403, the HTML endpoint needs JavaScript, headless browsers get detected), so replacement engines need testing; and the license is AGPL-3.0-or-later, whose exact terms should be checked for the intended deployment. The README specifically discusses source obligations for a modified network-service version; network access alone is not a complete licence analysis.

...

What it is: 19 lessons, four hands-on exercises, Markdown sources, a single-file offline HTML reader, and scripts to build and verify publication. The order follows the engineering chain: agent landscape, LLMs for builders, RAG, tool use and function calling, orchestration, context management, memory architecture, multi-agent systems, system optimisation, evaluation engineering, data selection and quality, LLM judges, safety, coding agents, proactive agents, open problems.

signals.title: Google and Meta Open-source TorchTPU to Bring Native PyTorch Support to Google TPUs - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
TorchTPU is an open-source project developed by Google in collaboration with Meta that provides a native PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables PyTorch workloads to execute on TPU hardware with minimal code modifications, supporting eager and compiled execution, distributed computing, and hardware-specific optimizations.

...

Specifically, migrating from GPUs to TPUs involves replacing the `cuda` device with `tpu` and the `nccl` distributed backend with `tpu_dist`. Alternatively, developers can use the new `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator` API to identify the available accelerator, as shown in the following snippet.

...

TorchTPU support three eager execution modes: strict, debug, and DeferAndFuse. The latter is a new hybrid eager/compiled execution mode that Google claims "can be 50% or more faster than Strict Eager while reducing peak HBM memory".

...

To validate TorchTPU's performance, Google ran a 30-billion parameter Muse Glimmer model implemented in standard PyTorch. On a single TPUv7 chip, inference throughput reached 25.7k token/s at 5120 sequence length and 22.4k token/s at 10,240 sequence length. For training, using four TPUv7 chips, throughput reached 5.6k token/s and 4.6k token/s at 5120 and 10,240 sequence length, respectively.

...

TorchTPU is still at an early stage and therefore in continuous evolution. The project's roadmap include work on dynamic shapes, compilation performance, operator coverage, reinforcement learning, and quantization. For further details, make sure to read the original announcement, which provides a more comprehensive view of TorchTPU's architecture and scope.
